context: Quraysh is Makkan and reads like an invoice presented to a tribe. The ilaf of Quraysh, their knitted-together security and covenanted trade, rested on their custodianship of the Ka’bah: because Arabia revered the House, the tribe of the House traveled unrobbed where others needed armed escort. On that safety ran the two great caravans, winter south to Yemen, summer north to Sham, greater Syria, and on those caravans ran Makkah’s food, wealth, and pride.

The surah names the whole arrangement and then presents the bill: fal-ya’budu rabba hadha al-bayt, so let them worship the Lord of this House, who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear. Quraysh were consuming the House’s blessings while rejecting the House’s Lord and persecuting His Messenger ﷺ. For the early community the surah distilled worldly wellbeing to its two irreducible elements, food and safety, and taught that both are gifts with a Giver, and the Giver has an address they already knew.
name_story: The surah is named for Quraysh, the Prophet’s ﷺ own tribe, the only surah in the Quran titled with a tribe’s name. It is also cited as Li-ilafi Quraysh from its opening phrase, and some reports describe early codices writing it joined closely to Al-Fil, so tightly the two arguments run as one.

movements.note: The knitted security of Quraysh, their winter journey and summer journey, is held up as the visible miracle they lived on every year without wondering who guaranteed the roads.
The conclusion is one command with two receipts: worship the Lord of this House, the One who fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear.

themes.d: The surah pairs food and safety as the twin floors of civilization: markets, journeys, and families all stand on two gifts most people never audit.
Rabba hadha al-bayt, the Lord of this House: not the House, not the tribe, not the trade routes. Blessing traced honestly leads to One door.
Quraysh thought their treaties and reputation secured the caravans; the surah shows the guarantee was always divine, dispensed through the House they were misusing.
Fal-ya’budu, so let them worship: the surah’s only command. Every enjoyed mercy is an unanswered summons until worship answers it.

heart: Quraysh is a small surah that performs a large audit on the reciter. Its method is to take the two blessings so constant they have become invisible, the meal that came without famine and the night that passed without fear, and hold them up as debts. Read slowly, verse four turns any ordinary day inside out: you ate, and you were safe, therefore two receipts are already on the table before you have done anything at all. The heart that absorbs this cannot treat worship as a favor it does Allah; worship becomes the barest honesty about how one is being carried.

There is also a tender specificity in rabba hadha al-bayt, the Lord of this House. Allah names Himself through the place He gave them, as if to say: you know where to find Me; you have circled My House your whole lives. For the reciter, the phrase gathers every qiblah-facing prayer into an answer to this surah’s command.

passages.why: The surah’s single command, worship aimed at the Lord of the House you already face five times a day.
Two receipts that cover every ordinary day: fed against hunger, secured against fear.

connections.why: Al-Fil shows the rescue of the House; Quraysh presents the obligation the rescue created, two surahs forming one argument.
Surah Ibrahim carries the ancestor’s prayer, a secure city and provision for its people, which these four verses show fully answered.

virtue.text: No authentic hadith singles out Quraysh with a recitation reward; reports of special equivalence for it are not sound. It needs no certificate: it is the Quran’s shortest complete lesson on gratitude for food and safety.
